     7	`wiki/` is **what is true about this company** — the graph, the tables, the events, what
     8	we have already measured, what we have read.
     9	
    10	`.claude/skills/` is **what we have learned to do here** — connecting to the warehouse,
    11	the estimator that works when a display rule rather than randomisation decides exposure,
    12	how a result gets written up so people here act on it. The inventory is
    13	`.claude/SKILLS.md`, and it says how a skill earns its way from staging into trusted.
    14	
    15	Neither was written in advance. **Both accumulate from real questions, and they
    16	accumulate together**: a question adds facts to the wiki and, when the work was genuinely
    17	novel, a procedure to the skills. A question that leaves both unchanged was a wasted
    18	question.
    19	
    20	| Folder | What lives there | Written when |
    21	|---|---|---|
    22	| `concepts/` | **The causal graph.** One file per variable. | During interviews |
    23	| `tables/` | Semantic layer: tables, columns, grains, joins, filters, gotchas | Ingest |
    24	| `events/` | What the company changed, and when | Interviews and ingest |
    25	| `processes/` | How the business actually works, in prose | Ingest and interviews |
    26	| `experiments/` | Past tests, what they found, **and the priors they hand you** | Ingest and close |
    27	| `methods/` | **How we measure things here.** Standing methodology, reviewed | When a methodology question is settled |
    28	| `literature/` | **What the field says.** Papers, library docs, other companies | Ingest |
    29	| `traps/` | Mistakes that keep happening here | After questions |
    30	| `questions/` | One folder per question: record, notebook or report, result | The whole lifecycle |
    31	| `questions/INDEX.md` | **One line per question. The entry point.** | At ask, and at close |
    32	
    33	Templates for each are in `_templates/`.
    34	
    35	## Finding a question again a month later
    36	
    37	Nobody says "q-0042" out loud. They say "that Avios thing", or "what Priya asked before
    38	the offsite". Three mechanisms, all cheap, and they only work if they are kept up:
    39	
    40	1. **`questions/INDEX.md`** — one line each, and a single file read. Look here first,
    41	   before assuming a question is new.
    42	2. **`aliases:` in the question frontmatter** — the words people actually use, written the
    43	   way they say them. This is what makes grep work later.
    44	3. **`{q:q-0042 on:2026-09-06}` on anything a question wrote** — the same visible span the
    45	   graph uses for edges. One convention, both jobs.
    46	
    47	And when something arrives after the fact — the test ran, the stakeholders decided, the
    48	estimate turned out wrong — it goes into that question's `## Outcome log`, dated,
    49	append-only, via `/cb_outcome`. **A concluded question is not closed to evidence.**
    50	
    51	## The graph
    52	
    53	One markdown file per variable in `concepts/`. The headings carry direction and kind —
    54	Obsidian's graph view has neither, so the structure has to.
    55	
    56	- `## Caused by` — incoming causal edge
    57	- `## Causes` — outgoing causal edge
    58	- `## Computed from` — **arithmetic only**, never causal
    59	
    60	An edge may be declared from either end. Each bullet is a wikilink, one line of
    61	reasoning, and a `{by:... on:...}` span recording who confirmed it. No span means
    62	nobody has confirmed it yet.
    63	
    64	`measured_at` in the frontmatter is the most valuable field in the wiki. It is what
    65	stops a mediator being used as a control, and no semantic layer records it.
    66	
    67	## Concepts vs columns
    68	
    69	A **concept** is a causal variable and gets a node file. A **column** is one physical
    70	place it is stored and lives on a table page. Many columns, one concept.
    71	
    72	Merge two columns into one concept only if a causal claim about one is a causal claim
    73	about the other: same quantity, same grain, same timing. `churn_30d` and `churn_90d`
    74	are two concepts, not one — different timing, and they can sit on opposite ends of the
    75	same edge.
    76	
    77	**Do not create a concept for every column.** A column becomes a concept when a
    78	question needs it in a graph. Most never will.
    79	
    80	## Named graphs
    81	
    82	`graphs: [pricing, retention]` in the frontmatter. A company has many loosely-connected
    83	causal areas and one big graph is unreadable. Membership is declared in the node, never
    84	in a separate list, so nothing can fall out of sync.
    85	
    86	## Methods and experiments get read *before* the graph
    87	
    88	Two folders answer questions that are not about any one dataset.
    89	
    90	`methods/` is the company's standing answer to "how should we measure this?" —
    91	incrementality, holdout design, when a contextual bandit beats a fixed A/B test, what
    92	MMM is and is not good for. Some have a notebook behind them, some are a white paper,
    93	some are one hard-won paragraph. Every page carries `tags: [method]` and lists the
    94	questions that used it, so a technique and the artefacts built with it stay linked in
    95	both directions.
    96	
    97	A method is **amended, never quietly replaced.** It binds every future question, so a
    98	change to one is proposed, reviewed and confirmed the way a causal edge is.
    99	
   100	Every method page carries **`evidence:`** as well as `status:`, and they are different
   101	claims. `status: established` means everyone here follows it. `evidence: none-yet` means
   102	nothing has tested it — the honest and common state for a design that stakeholders
   103	approved before it ran. Such a method binds future questions **as a convention, not as a
   104	finding**, and says so on its face. When something finally runs, the page is amended and
   105	`evidence:` moves to `ran-once`, then `replicated`. A design that turned out wrong is
   106	amended too, and that amendment is worth more than the original page.
   107	
   108	`literature/` is everything read from outside: DoWhy or Meridian documentation, a paper
   109	worth keeping, a blog post from a company with our problem. Each page records the claim
   110	*stated precisely enough to be wrong*, what it assumes, what it does **not** cover, and a
   111	trust level with a reason. The `scholar` agent reads this folder before answering
   112	anything methodological, and it marks its own claims `[lib]` or `[bg]` so a citation is
   113	never confused with a recollection.
   114	
   115	`experiments/` is what we have already measured. Read it before designing anything. A
   116	randomised estimate is a **prior**: fitting a parameter freely when an experiment
   117	already measured it throws away the best evidence in the building. This is the whole
   118	reason the folder exists — asked for an MMM, the channel priors should come from the
   119	geo tests and holdouts recorded here, not from a default.
   120	
   121	## Seeing the graph in Obsidian
   122	
   123	Every file in `concepts/` carries `tags: [dag]`. **Nothing else in the wiki carries it.**
   124	That single tag is the whole mechanism: type `tag:#dag` into the graph view's search box
   125	and the tables, events, processes and question records drop away, leaving the causal
   126	graph on its own.
   127	
   128	`wiki/methods/` carries `tags: [method]` and `wiki/literature/` carries
   129	`tags: [literature]`, on the same principle. Swap the search box to `tag:#method` for the
   130	methodology layer or `tag:#literature` for what we have read.
   131	
   132	**Three tags, three layers: what is true here, how we measure it, what the field says.**
   133	Stop there. The headings already carry direction and kind, and a fourth tag vocabulary
   134	that duplicates them will drift out of sync with them.
   135	
   136	## Finding things
   137	
   138	Grep. `rg "churn" wiki/`, `rg "measured_at: post_treatment" wiki/concepts/`,
   139	`rg -l "pricing" wiki/concepts/`. The wiki is small enough that search is reading.
   140

1	# Pay with Avios — BA Holidays
     2	
     3	How the product works, as described by the analyst. Facts only; causal claims found in
     4	the source are quarantined at the bottom of this page as attributed prose.
     5	
     6	Source: `raw/pwa_exp` (same text previously ingested as `raw/iagl_pwa`),
     7	recorded_by: analyst, recorded_on: 2026-09-07.
     8	
     9	## The company and the product
    10	
    11	IAG Loyalty (IAGL) is the company behind the **Avios** loyalty currency. One of its
    12	products is **Pay with Avios (PWA) for BA Holidays**: when a member is booking a holiday
    13	they can redeem some of their Avios for a discount on the holiday ticket.
    14	
    15	BA Holidays is now part of IAGL. BA Holidays' own margin on a booking is **10% of the
    16	ticket price**. {source: raw/pwa_exp}
    17	
    18	## The discount ladder
    19	
    20	At booking the member is presented with **up to 9 discount options**. Each option is:
    21	
    22	- a **percentage of the ticket price** taken as discount, and
    23	- an **Avios-to-cash conversion rate** attached to that discount tier.
    24	
    25	The conversion rate ranges from **0.01** (most favourable to the member — each Avios buys
    26	more discount) down to **0.004** (least favourable).
    27	
    28	Under normal policy the ladder is **penalising**: the higher the discount tier, the worse
    29	the conversion rate. That mapping was inverted for two weeks in August 2026 — see
    30	[[2026-08-conversion-rate-flip-experiment]].
    31	
    32	## Key business metrics
    33	
    34	Defined on the source's own words; see [[iagl-pwa-metrics]] for the formulas.
    35	
    36	- Number of bookings made using the product
    37	- Avios redeemed
    38	- Cash (cash paid on the booking)
    39	- Cost per Avios = sum of cash in the window ÷ sum of Avios in the window
    40	
    41	## What is and is not observable
    42	
    43	**This is the central data limitation of the product.**
    44	
    45	- Visible: all *logged-in member* activity — searches and bookings.
    46	- **Not visible: BA Holidays booking volume independent of Avios use.** Non-member
    47	  bookings are hidden from IAGL. {source: raw/pwa_exp}
    48	
    49	So the denominator "all BA Holidays bookings" does not exist in our data. Any metric
    50	phrased as a *share* of total BA Holidays bookings is not computable as stated, and any
    51	design that needs untreated non-member bookings as a control group is unavailable.
    52	
    53	## Causal claims made in the source (attributed, not edges)
    54	
    55	These are the business's model of the product. They are **not** drawn in
    56	`wiki/concepts/` — edges are only drawn in an interview where the analyst confirms them.
    57	
    58	- The August 2026 experiment rationale argued that a **more attractive conversion rate on
    59	  the high-discount tiers would drive more bookings**, and that the extra volume — counted
    60	  against the *combined* IAGL + BA Holidays margin — would keep overall margin high
    61	  despite a higher short-run redemption cost. {source: raw/pwa_exp}
    62	- The source describes marginal margin as "usually very small", because cost per Avios
    63	  typically sits around **0.005** against an Avios value of 0.00659. {source: raw/pwa_exp}
    64

1	# IAGL Pay-with-Avios metric definitions
     2	
     3	Definitions exactly as given by the analyst. Source: `raw/pwa_exp`, recorded_by: analyst,
     4	recorded_on: 2026-09-07.
     5	
     6	These are **arithmetic identities**, not causal statements. If any of these quantities
     7	becomes a node in a graph, the relationship between it and its inputs belongs under
     8	`## Computed from`, never `## Caused by`.
     9	
    10	## Cost per Avios (CPA)
    11	
    12	    cost_per_avios = sum(cash in window) / sum(avios in window)
    13	
    14	Typical observed level: **around 0.005**. {source: raw/pwa_exp}
    15	
    16	Note the window dependence: CPA is a ratio of two sums over a chosen period, not a
    17	per-booking average. Changing the window changes the number.
    18	
    19	## IAGL margin
    20	
    21	    iagl_margin = sum(avios redeemed in period) * 0.00659 - sum(cash in period)
    22	
    23	0.00659 is the internal value placed on one Avios. Because CPA is usually ~0.005 against
    24	a 0.00659 valuation, the marginal margin per redemption is small.
    25	
    26	## Combined IAGL + BA Holidays margin
    27	
    28	BA Holidays is part of IAGL and takes **10% of the ticket price** as its own margin. The
    29	August 2026 experiment was justified on a *combined* margin basis:
    30	
    31	    combined_margin = iagl_margin + 0.10 * sum(ticket price in period)
    32	
    33	This combined formula is the one the experiment's business case rested on. It is recorded
    34	here as the definition used; whether it was the right basis is a question, not a fact.
    35	
    36	## Volume metrics
    37	
    38	- **Bookings made using the product** — bookings where Avios were redeemed. Bookings made
    39	  without Avios, and all non-member bookings, are not visible; see
    40	  [[pay-with-avios-ba-holidays]].
    41	- **Avios redeemed** and **cash** — the two components of every metric above.

    14	## What changed
    15	The mapping between discount tier and conversion rate was flipped for the two-week
    16	window. Normally the **maximum discount** tier carries the **least favourable**
    17	conversion rate for the member (down to 0.004) and the **minimum discount** tier the
    18	**most favourable** (up to 0.01). During the experiment window this was inverted: the
    19	max discount became the *most* favourable conversion rate, and the min discount the
    20	*least* favourable.
    21	
    22	Rationale given: this was expected to be costly to IAGL/BA Holidays in the short run —
    23	treated as an investment intended to drive more bookings and, via the combined IAGL + BA
    24	Holidays margin (BA Holidays keeps ~10% of ticket price on top of IAGL's Avios margin),
    25	keep overall margin high despite the richer redemption terms.

    28	All members, all routes — but **only for bookings with a future departure date within
    29	2026**.
    30	
    31	## Who it did NOT apply to
    32	Bookings with departure dates in 2027 or later kept the standard (non-flipped)
    33	conversion rate schedule. This is the only segmentation boundary recorded — there was no
    34	member-level or route-level split.
    35	
    36	## Why it matters causally
    37	This was **not a randomised A/B test** — there is no A/B split of members or bookings;
    38	the policy applied uniformly to everyone booking a 2026 departure. The only exploitable
    39	boundary is the departure-date cutoff (within-2026 vs 2027+), which is a plausible
    40	regression-discontinuity/DiD-style comparison group, not a randomised control.

    42	Announcement timing is not stated in the source — unknown whether members anticipated
    43	the change. Flagged as unclassified/unknown, see ingest summary.

    46	A same-period-last-year (Aug 2025) DiD counterfactual was attempted and found to be

     2	
     3	The other half of this system. `wiki/` records **what is true about this company**; these

     5	accumulate from real questions.

     8	close, and by `technician` when it builds access.
     9	
    10	**Read this before opening a question.** What we can already do changes what is worth
    11	proposing: an existing warehouse connection makes `live` data cheap rather than a
    12	project, and an existing estimator for a shape of problem that recurs here means the
    13	analysis is mostly written already.
    14	
    15	| skill | kind | standing | used on | what it is for |
    16	|---|---|---|---|---|
    17	| *(example)* `snowflake-holdout-pull` | ACCESS | staging | q-0031 | assembling a treated/control table from the warehouse |

    21	
    22	- **ACCESS** — reaching a system. Warehouse connections, API clients, export paths,
    23	  wherever a result has to land. `technician` owns these.

    25	  for a problem shape that recurs here, what varies between instances of it, and what was
    26	  tried first that did not work.
    27	- **REPORTING** — how a result gets written up so people here actually act on it.

    30	
    31	- **staging** — `.claude/skills-staging/`. Captured from one question, unproven. Offered
    32	  when it looks relevant; never assumed.

    34	  one question**, or by having its output **checked mechanically** — the notebook ran
    35	  clean and its assertions held.

    41	wrong. A system that promoted skills because stakeholders liked the output would get

# Skill: drawing-the-dag (trusted) — .claude/skills/drawing-the-dag/SKILL.md

---
name: drawing-the-dag
description: How to write causal structure into wiki/concepts — creating nodes, adding edges, marking observability and timing. Use during interviews whenever structure is being established.
---

# Drawing the graph

The graph is markdown files in `wiki/concepts/`, one per variable. It is the thing every
verdict is computed from, so it is worth getting the mechanics exactly right.

## Before you create a node, look for it

**Read `wiki/concepts/` and check whether this quantity already has one.** Match on
`label:` and the prose, not just the filename — the same variable arrives wearing a
different word every time somebody new asks about it. "Drop-off", "leavers", "attrition"
and `churn_30d` might be one node or four, and getting that wrong is the main way this
graph rots into something nobody trusts.

The test from `wiki/README.md` decides it: **same quantity, same grain, same timing** is
one concept. If any of the three differs they are two — `churn_30d` and `churn_90d` are
genuinely separate and can sit at opposite ends of the same edge.

If it exists, **extend it**: add the edge, add what was learned, add the backlink. Do not
create a near-duplicate because the existing node is named awkwardly; rename it if the
analyst agrees, or live with the name.

If it does not exist, create it — and say so in the conversation, so the analyst can
object to the name now rather than in a year when six things point at it.

## A node

```markdown
---
id: churn_30d
label: 30-day churn
observed: true
measured_at: post_treatment
graphs: [retention, pricing]
tags: [dag]
source: interview/2026-03-04
confirmed_by: guido
confirmed_on: 2026-03-04
---

## Caused by
- [[price_change]] — repricing shifts cancellation within the billing cycle. {by:guido on:2026-03-04}

## Causes
- [[net_revenue]] {by:guido on:2026-03-04}

## Computed from
- [[cancellations_30d]], [[active_base]] — ratio.

Prose. What this actually is. The gotcha nobody remembers.
```

The **heading carries direction and kind.** Obsidian's graph view is undirected and
untyped, so wikilinks alone are not enough — that is why the structure does the work.

## The three headings

`## Caused by` — incoming causal. `## Causes` — outgoing causal. Declare an edge from
either end; both are valid.

`## Computed from` — **arithmetic only.** `net_revenue = revenue × (1 − churn)` is
exactly true and carries zero causal content. It must never appear under a causal
heading, because a path running through arithmetic edges makes an accounting identity
look like a finding, and that error is invisible once it is in the graph.

## The three fields that matter most

**`measured_at`** — before or after the thing we are calling treatment. This is what
stops a mediator being used as a control. No semantic layer records it; it comes from
the analyst, in conversation, and it is the most valuable field in the wiki.

**`observed`** — `false` is a *claim*, and it needs a `source`. It is also the material
refusals are made of: an unobserved node on an unblockable backdoor path is exactly what
makes a question unanswerable, and naming it is what makes the refusal useful.

**`graphs`** — which named areas this belongs to. Membership lives in the node, never in
a separate manifest, so nothing can fall out of sync.

## The `{...}` span

`{by:guido on:2026-03-04}` after the reasoning. **No span means nobody has confirmed
this edge** — it is a proposal, and any verdict resting on it is provisional.

Visible rather than an HTML comment, deliberately: provenance you cannot see is
provenance nobody maintains, and a hidden marker breaks the moment someone hand-edits
the file in a text editor.

## Rules

**Every node gets `tags: [dag]`, and nothing else in the wiki does.** It exists for one
purpose: filtering the Obsidian graph view to `tag:#dag` so the causal graph can be seen
without the tables, events and question records on top of it. Do not invent further tags
— the headings already carry direction and kind.

**Adding an edge during an interview is fine.** The analyst is right there.

**Changing a confirmed edge means asking.** Reversing something confirmed last month is
a claim that the earlier judgement was wrong, and it may invalidate a past analysis.
Stop and say so.

**Deleting a node or edge always means asking.**

**The reasoning line is not decoration.** It is what a future session uses to decide
whether the edge still holds. "Because the billing cycle means a price change lands
within 30 days" survives; "obviously related" does not.

**One concept per causal variable, not per column.** If two columns in different tables
mean the same quantity at the same grain with the same timing, they are one concept with
two places it is stored. If any of those three differ, they are two concepts.

content.text:
Seven nodes written into `wiki/concepts/` — the first graph here, under `graph: pwa-pricing`.

**Where the graph stands**

- **Treatment** `pwa_conversion_rate_flip`, fully determined by two pre-treatment facts: `booking_in_flip_window` and `departure_year_within_2026`. Assignment is a **deterministic rule**, not randomisation — and confirmed as such.
- **Outcome** is now `member_booking_volume` (all member bookings), with `avios_redeeming_bookings` as a subset beneath it. The split between them is `## Computed from` — arithmetic — so a shift in redemption mix is explicitly *not* a finding about volume. That guard is now in the wiki.
- **Main threat** is `booking_departure_lead_time`: it sits upstream of both the assignment variable and the outcome, and it encodes your "different kind of trip". This is a parallel-trends problem, not a classic confounder — nothing about lead time caused the policy.
- **`seasonal_holiday_demand`** is marked `observed: false` as a *proposal*, needing a source. It only breaks the design if it moved 2026 and 2027 departures **differently** in that fortnight; if it moved them together, DiD absorbs it.
- Shape of the answer: difference-in-differences across the departure-year boundary, on total member bookings, with the redeeming/non-redeeming split as the substitution check — and the Aug-2025 route explicitly ruled out as already-known-biased.

**What remains:** one event sweep, then it's testable. Anticipation effects I can test in the notebook rather than ask about.

Interview complete. Four exchanges, analyst proceeded.

**(a) Concept files written** — first graph in this wiki, all `graph: pwa-pricing`, all `tags: [dag]`:

- `wiki/concepts/pwa_conversion_rate_flip.md` (treatment)
- `wiki/concepts/booking_in_flip_window.md`
- `wiki/concepts/departure_year_within_2026.md`
- `wiki/concepts/member_booking_volume.md` (outcome)
- `wiki/concepts/avios_redeeming_bookings.md`
- `wiki/concepts/booking_departure_lead_time.md`
- `wiki/concepts/seasonal_holiday_demand.md` (`observed: false`, proposal)
- `wiki/concepts/avios_balance.md`

Also corrected, because the interview overturned them: `wiki/processes/pay-with-avios-ba-holidays.md` and `wiki/experiments/2026-08-conversion-rate-flip.md` — the invisible group is **non-members**, not non-redeemers. And `wiki/questions/q-0001/q-0001.md` updated (`data_mode: simulated`, `delivery: staged`, `run_here: true`, `dag_tested: no`, `deliverable:` left null for you to ask).

**(b) The graph, in prose.** Exposure to the flip is a deterministic function of two pre-treatment facts: the booking fell in 1–14 August 2026, and its departure date is inside 2026. There is no member or route split, so this is a rule, not randomisation. The flip is taken to raise `avios_redeeming_bookings` (that is the mechanism, and it is spanned as confirmed); whether it raises `member_booking_volume` is the hypothesis and is deliberately left **unspanned**, because stamping it would assume the answer. `member_booking_volume` is `## Computed from` redeeming plus non-redeeming bookings — arithmetic — so a shift in redemption mix can never be presented as incremental volume. The threat runs through `booking_departure_lead_time`, which is caused by the departure-year boundary and causes booking volume: it is not a classic confounder (nothing about lead time caused the policy) but it makes treated and control structurally different. `seasonal_holiday_demand` is unobserved and only bites if it moved the two departure-year groups differently in that fortnight. Critically, there is **no** edge from the flip back to departure year — the analyst ruled out pull-forward, so the control group is genuinely untreated.

**(c) Proposed identification.** Difference-in-differences across the departure-date boundary — bookings departing within 2026 (treated) versus 2027+ (untreated) — on **total member booking volume**, using booking date as the time dimension with a pre-period in July 2026 and a post-period after 14 August. The Aug-2025 year-on-year counterfactual is ruled out up front as already-known-biased by the unnamed 2025 change. The parallel-trends assumption is the whole load-bearing assumption and must be tested on pre-window booking dates, not assumed; event-study leads and lags around 1 and 14 August double as the anticipation test that answers the unknown announcement date. Alongside the volume estimate, run the same DiD on the redeeming/non-redeeming split as a **substitution check**: a large move in redeeming bookings with no move in total member bookings is the flip changing how holidays are paid for, not creating any, and that is the most likely true outcome. Under `simulated` this recovers a planted effect and proves the machinery — it says nothing about IAGL.

**(d) For the reviewer to stress-test:**

1. **Is parallel trends defensible at all** when the analyst's own words are that 2027 departures are "a different kind of trip with almost no overlap"? That is the exact reason the groups may not trend together. Should this be DiD on levels, on logs, or a synthetic control built from finer departure-month cohorts?
2. **Is the boundary sharp or arbitrary?** A departure on 28 Dec 2026 and one on 3 Jan 2027 are nearly the same trip. Does an RD-in-departure-date around 31 December beat a whole-group DiD, and is there enough density there?
3. **Composition change inside the treated group.** The flip changes which *discount tier* members pick, so the treated group's booking mix may change even if volume does not. Does that contaminate the outcome?
4. **The unspanned hypothesis edge.** Is it legitimate to leave flip → `member_booking_volume` unconfirmed while treating flip → `avios_redeeming_bookings` as confirmed mechanism, or does that asymmetry bias the design?
5. **Unobserved `seasonal_holiday_demand`** — is "the analyst knows of nothing else" enough, or does the design need a placebo (e.g. non-BA-Holidays member activity, or the same DiD on a window where no flip occurred)?
6. **Whether any of this is worth doing given power.** Two weeks, one market. Would a minimum detectable effect calculation kill the design before the estimator does?

    14	## What changed

    17	conversion rate for the member (down to 0.004) and the **minimum discount** tier the

    33	conversion rate schedule. This is the only segmentation boundary recorded — there was no

1	# Pay with Avios — BA Holidays
     2	
     3	How the product works, as described by the analyst. Facts only; causal claims found in
     4	the source are quarantined at the bottom of this page as attributed prose.
     5	
     6	Source: `raw/pwa_exp` (same text previously ingested as `raw/iagl_pwa`),
     7	recorded_by: analyst, recorded_on: 2026-09-07.
     8	
     9	## The company and the product
    10	
    11	IAG Loyalty (IAGL) is the company behind the **Avios** loyalty currency. One of its
    12	products is **Pay with Avios (PWA) for BA Holidays**: when a member is booking a holiday
    13	they can redeem some of their Avios for a discount on the holiday ticket.
    14	
    15	BA Holidays is now part of IAGL. BA Holidays' own margin on a booking is **10% of the
    16	ticket price**. {source: raw/pwa_exp}
    17	
    18	## The discount ladder
    19	
    20	At booking the member is presented with **up to 9 discount options**. Each option is:
    21	
    22	- a **percentage of the ticket price** taken as discount, and
    23	- an **Avios-to-cash conversion rate** attached to that discount tier.
    24	
    25	The conversion rate ranges from **0.01** (most favourable to the member — each Avios buys
    26	more discount) down to **0.004** (least favourable).
    27	
    28	Under normal policy the ladder is **penalising**: the higher the discount tier, the worse
    29	the conversion rate. That mapping was inverted for two weeks in August 2026 — see
    30	[[2026-08-conversion-rate-flip-experiment]].
    31	
    32	## Key business metrics
    33	
    34	Defined on the source's own words; see [[iagl-pwa-metrics]] for the formulas.
    35	
    36	- Number of bookings made using the product
    37	- Avios redeemed
    38	- Cash (cash paid on the booking)
    39	- Cost per Avios = sum of cash in the window ÷ sum of Avios in the window
    40	
    41	## What is and is not observable
    42	
    43	**This is the central data limitation of the product.**
    44	
    45	- Visible: all *logged-in member* activity — searches and **all member bookings, whether
    46	  or not Avios were redeemed**. Avios-redeeming bookings are a strict subset of visible
    47	  member bookings. Confirmed by the analyst in interview. {q:q-0001 on:2026-09-07}
    48	- **Not visible: non-member BA Holidays bookings.** These are hidden from IAGL.
    49	  {source: raw/pwa_exp}
    50	
    51	Correction: an earlier reading of `raw/pwa_exp` implied that only Avios-redeeming
    52	bookings were countable. That was wrong. The invisible group is **non-members**, not
    53	non-redeemers. {q:q-0001 on:2026-09-07}
    54	
    55	Consequences:
    56	
    57	- The denominator "all BA Holidays bookings" still does not exist in our data, so any
    58	  metric phrased as a share of *total* BA Holidays bookings is not computable as stated,
    59	  and non-member bookings are unavailable as a control group.
    60	- But **member booking volume is an observable outcome**, and it can be decomposed into
    61	  redeeming and non-redeeming bookings. This is what lets a genuine increase in bookings
    62	  be told apart from members merely switching into redeeming on bookings they would have
    63	  made anyway. That distinction is the crux of q-0001.
    64	
    65	## Causal claims made in the source (attributed, not edges)
    66	
    67	These are the business's model of the product. They are **not** drawn in
    68	`wiki/concepts/` — edges are only drawn in an interview where the analyst confirms them.
    69	
    70	- The August 2026 experiment rationale argued that a **more attractive conversion rate on
    71	  the high-discount tiers would drive more bookings**, and that the extra volume — counted
    72	  against the *combined* IAGL + BA Holidays margin — would keep overall margin high
    73	  despite a higher short-run redemption cost. {source: raw/pwa_exp}
    74	- The source describes marginal margin as "usually very small", because cost per Avios
    75	  typically sits around **0.005** against an Avios value of 0.00659. {source: raw/pwa_exp}

1	# IAGL Pay-with-Avios metric definitions
     2	
     3	Definitions exactly as given by the analyst. Source: `raw/pwa_exp`, recorded_by: analyst,
     4	recorded_on: 2026-09-07.
     5	
     6	These are **arithmetic identities**, not causal statements. If any of these quantities
     7	becomes a node in a graph, the relationship between it and its inputs belongs under
     8	`## Computed from`, never `## Caused by`.
     9	
    10	## Cost per Avios (CPA)
    11	
    12	    cost_per_avios = sum(cash in window) / sum(avios in window)
    13	
    14	Typical observed level: **around 0.005**. {source: raw/pwa_exp}
    15	
    16	Note the window dependence: CPA is a ratio of two sums over a chosen period, not a
    17	per-booking average. Changing the window changes the number.
    18	
    19	## IAGL margin
    20	
    21	    iagl_margin = sum(avios redeemed in period) * 0.00659 - sum(cash in period)
    22	
    23	0.00659 is the internal value placed on one Avios. Because CPA is usually ~0.005 against
    24	a 0.00659 valuation, the marginal margin per redemption is small.
    25	
    26	## Combined IAGL + BA Holidays margin
    27	
    28	BA Holidays is part of IAGL and takes **10% of the ticket price** as its own margin. The
    29	August 2026 experiment was justified on a *combined* margin basis:
    30	
    31	    combined_margin = iagl_margin + 0.10 * sum(ticket price in period)
    32	
    33	This combined formula is the one the experiment's business case rested on. It is recorded
    34	here as the definition used; whether it was the right basis is a question, not a fact.
    35	
    36	## Volume metrics
    37	
    38	- **Bookings made using the product** — bookings where Avios were redeemed. Bookings made
    39	  without Avios, and all non-member bookings, are not visible; see
    40	  [[pay-with-avios-ba-holidays]].
    41	- **Avios redeemed** and **cash** — the two components of every metric above.

Reviewed: `wiki/questions/q-0001/q-0001.md`, all 8 nodes of `graph: pwa-pricing`, `wiki/processes/pay-with-avios-ba-holidays.md`, `wiki/processes/iagl-pwa-metrics.md`, `wiki/events/2026-08-conversion-rate-flip-experiment.md`, `wiki/experiments/2026-08-conversion-rate-flip.md`. `wiki/methods/` and `wiki/traps/` are empty — no standing method is contradicted, and no past experiment answers this (the only experiment page deliberately records **no** prior).

**(a) Adjustment does not identify this, and the graph shows why.** The backdoor path is

Both `departure_year_within_2026` and `booking_departure_lead_time` are `observed: true` and `measured_at: pre_treatment`, so the path is nominally blockable. But `departure_year_within_2026` **is** the assignment rule: conditioning on it removes every drop of treatment variation. Positivity fails exactly where the confounding lives. Same for lead time, which is a deterministic descendant of departure year within the window. **So do not put `booking_departure_lead_time` in any adjustment set** — it is collinear with the group indicator and conditioning on it strips the comparison rather than cleaning it. There is no adjustment-based identification here and there never will be.

**(b) DiD is therefore the right family, and its assumption is invisible to the DAG.** Parallel trends is a restriction on counterfactual *trends*, not on edges; no DAG expresses it. That means the graph cannot bless this design and cannot refuse it. It has to be earned empirically, and the record currently does not have enough pre-period to earn it.

Nothing in the proposed adjustment set is post-treatment. The outcome is **not** an accounting identity — the treatment→outcome path does not run through `## Computed from` edges. But note the trap sitting one step away: `avios_redeeming_bookings` is a subset of the outcome, and `iagl-pwa-metrics.md` defines "bookings made using the product" as redeeming bookings only. **An effect on redeeming bookings reported as an effect on booking volume is arithmetic dressed as a finding.** That is the single most likely way this question gets misread by a stakeholder.

**`data_mode: simulated`.** No number this produces says anything about IAGL. It can show the code runs, that the estimator recovers a planted effect, and — most valuably — what effect size the design could detect. It cannot show the flip did or did not create bookings. Any write-up must carry that on its face, and nothing from it may enter `wiki/experiments/` as a prior.

## The six stress tests

**1. Parallel trends across "a different kind of trip".** The analyst's own words are close to a refutation of the *level* DiD. Near-term 2026 departures booked in August are peak-season, high-volume, short-lead; 2027 departures booked in August are a thin, flat, long-lead series. A common multiplicative shock (weather, macro, competitor pricing, a pay week) then produces very different absolute movements, and the DiD reads the difference as effect. Recommendations, in order of strength:

- **Do not run this in levels.** Use a log or Poisson/log-link DiD so the assumption becomes *common proportional* trends, which is the assumption the business story actually implies. Say on the page which scale you are claiming — log-DiD and level-DiD are different estimands and one can be flat while the other trends.
- **One pre-period month (July 2026) is the design's worst weakness and the most fixable one.** An event study with "leads" needs many pre-periods. Ask for 18–24 months of booking-date series, and check ratio stability across all of it, not just the month before.
- **Replace the lumped "2027+" group with finer departure-month cohorts and let a synthetic control weight them** (booking-week × departure-month panel, donor pool = departure months outside 2026, pre-fit quality reported). A weighted donor set can match the treated cohorts' seasonal shape; a 1:1 comparison to "everything from 2027 onwards" cannot.
- **Better still, a control that is not a different kind of trip at all:** `avios_balance` is pre-treatment and gates whether the flip could bite. Members with near-zero balances cannot respond to a better conversion rate, so they are an untreated group *inside* the same trips and the same seasonality. A triple difference (departure-year group × period × can-respond) is the strongest design available here. It needs `avios_balance` to be genuinely observed — currently marked `observed: true` as an *assumption*, `confirmed_by: null`. That is worth one question to the analyst.

**2. Is the boundary sharp, and would RD beat DiD?** The rule is sharp; the *threshold* is arbitrary in exactly the way RD wants — a 30 Dec 2026 and a 3 Jan 2027 departure are nearly the same trip. So on comparability, RD in departure date around 31 Dec 2026 dominates the whole-group DiD. Two problems, one fatal on its own:

- The outcome is a **count of bookings by departure date**, so the density of the running variable *is* the outcome. You cannot use density continuity as the falsification test and the estimate at the same time, and manipulation (members shifting departure dates) is indistinguishable from effect. The graph asserts no such shifting — `pwa_conversion_rate_flip` records "no edge here, and it matters" — which helps, but it is one person's judgement, not a test.
- **31 December is the worst possible cutoff for seasonality.** Festive-peak departures against a January trough is a real discontinuity in demand that exists every year, flip or no flip.

The fix makes RD usable rather than discarding it: **difference-in-discontinuities.** Estimate the jump at 31 Dec using bookings made in the window, estimate the same jump using bookings made in the pre-period (July, and the same calendar weeks in earlier years), and difference them. The seasonal cliff is common to both and cancels. That is the design whose assumption you can actually check. Expect the density near the cutoff to be thin — bookings made in a 14-day window for departures within days of 31 Dec — so treat diff-in-disc as the **robustness check that would make the cohort synthetic control believable**, not as the headline.

**3. Composition inside the treated group.** Tier choice is *downstream* of treatment. For a count outcome it is a mediator, and it contaminates nothing **so long as you never condition on it**. Concretely: do not stratify by discount tier, do not restrict to redeeming bookings, do not weight by Avios redeemed or cost-per-Avios. Restricting to redeeming bookings conditions on a post-treatment variable and induces selection — that is the classic version of this error and it would look like a large effect.

The redeeming / non-redeeming split as a substitution check is legitimate **as a decomposition, reported as mix shift**, never as a second estimate of volume. And note the asymmetry: the non-redeeming series is post-treatment-selected too, so a fall in non-redeeming bookings is not evidence of cannibalisation unless read jointly with the total. The real compositional threat is different: if *which* members and trips book changes between pre and post inside the treated group, that is a violation of parallel trends dressed as composition. Fixed departure-month cohorts and a per-member outcome reduce it.

**4. Leaving `flip → member_booking_volume` unspanned.** Legitimate, and correct bookkeeping — that edge is the hypothesis, and stamping it confirmed would assume the answer. Two cautions:

- The pages disagree. `pwa_conversion_rate_flip.md` presents `flip → avios_redeeming_bookings` as confirmed mechanism with a `{by:analyst}` span; `avios_redeeming_bookings.md` records the same edge as "Proposed, not yet confirmed". One of the two needs correcting before anything rests on it.
- Because `member_booking_volume → avios_redeeming_bookings` also exists, the redeeming series cannot double as a check on volume. Use it for what it is good for: an **exposure / dose check**. If redeeming bookings did not move, the treatment did not land and no volume effect is credible. That is genuinely valuable and it is not evidence of incrementality.

**5. `seasonal_holiday_demand` is `observed: false`, and "nothing else changed" is not enough.** It is not enough for two reasons. First, it is absence-of-evidence from one person, recorded honestly as such on the node itself. Second, and more important, **seasonality is not "another change"** — it is always present, and it only needs to hit the two departure-year groups *differently* during 1–14 August to break the design. Belief cannot address that; placebos can. The design needs, and the record does not yet have:

- **Placebo windows** — the identical estimator on other 2-week booking windows through 2026 and on 1–14 Aug in years before the flip. The spread of those placebo estimates is the honest measure of uncertainty here.
- **Placebo outcome** — a member booking series the flip could not touch. Worth asking whether one exists (flight-only member bookings, non-PWA-eligible bookings).
- **Lead coefficients** in the event study, which also serve as the anticipation test the record already plans around 1 and 14 August. Good instinct; keep it. Announcement date unknown is handled correctly as a testable pattern rather than a blocking question.
- **Leave-one-cohort-out** for the synthetic control.

**6. Power. This is the most likely cause of death, and it is knowable before any estimator runs.** Two weeks, one policy, one treated group means **one treated cluster** — there is no valid cluster-robust standard error, and model-based SEs on a two-group panel will be badly optimistic. Inference must be permutation/randomisation inference over the placebo windows and placebo cohorts. Effective sample size is the number of *pre-periods*, not the number of bookings.

Order-of-magnitude, to be replaced by a real calculation: with a daily treated series whose residual day-to-day variation is 15–25% of its mean, 14 treated days gives a standard error around 4–7% of baseline, so an MDE at 80% power of roughly **11–20% lift** — before donor-fit error, which in practice inflates it. If the business would act on a 5% lift, this design cannot see it, and a null from it must never be reported as "no effect".

**The record does not state an MDE. That is a finding, and it should be the first cell of the notebook, not the last.** It is also the one place where a single company input transforms the exercise: the daily/weekly member booking counts and their volatility by departure-year group, for calibration. Everything else can stay simulated.

## What I would require before an analysis notebook is treated as a design

1. MDE stated, computed from calibrated counts, with permutation inference specified.
2. Pre-period extended to ≥18 months; the July-only pre-period abandoned.
3. Log/Poisson scale declared; levels dropped.
4. Departure-month cohorts as the panel, with synthetic-control weights over the donor pool, pre-fit reported.
5. Diff-in-discontinuity at 31 Dec 2026 as the comparability check

# Review — q-0001 (reviewer, 2026-09-07)

Reviewed: `wiki/questions/q-0001/q-0001.md`, all 8 nodes of `graph: pwa-pricing`, `wiki/processes/pay-with-avios-ba-holidays.md`, `wiki/processes/iagl-pwa-metrics.md`, `wiki/events/2026-08-conversion-rate-flip-experiment.md`, `wiki/experiments/2026-08-conversion-rate-flip.md`. `wiki/methods/` and `wiki/traps/` are empty — no standing method is contradicted, and no past experiment answers this (the only experiment page deliberately records **no** prior).

## Verdict

**IDENTIFIED UNDER STATED ASSUMPTIONS — and the assumption doing all the work is not one this graph can support.**

Two separate things must be said, because the record blurs them.

**(a) Adjustment does not identify this, and the graph shows why.** The backdoor path is
`pwa_conversion_rate_flip ← departure_year_within_2026 → booking_departure_lead_time → member_booking_volume`.
Both `departure_year_within_2026` and `booking_departure_lead_time` are `observed: true` and `measured_at: pre_treatment`, so the path is nominally blockable. But `departure_year_within_2026` **is** the assignment rule: conditioning on it removes every drop of treatment variation. Positivity fails exactly where the confounding lives. Same for lead time, which is a deterministic descendant of departure year within the window. **So do not put `booking_departure_lead_time` in any adjustment set** — it is collinear with the group indicator and conditioning on it strips the comparison rather than cleaning it. There is no adjustment-based identification here and there never will be.

**(b) DiD is therefore the right family, and its assumption is invisible to the DAG.** Parallel trends is a restriction on counterfactual *trends*, not on edges; no DAG expresses it. That means the graph cannot bless this design and cannot refuse it. It has to be earned empirically, and the record currently does not have enough pre-period to earn it.

Nothing in the proposed adjustment set is post-treatment. The outcome is **not** an accounting identity — the treatment→outcome path does not run through `## Computed from` edges. But note the trap sitting one step away: `avios_redeeming_bookings` is a subset of the outcome, and `iagl-pwa-metrics.md` defines "bookings made using the product" as redeeming bookings only. **An effect on redeeming bookings reported as an effect on booking volume is arithmetic dressed as a finding.** That is the single most likely way this question gets misread by a stakeholder.

**`data_mode: simulated`.** No number this produces says anything about IAGL. It can show the code runs, that the estimator recovers a planted effect, and — most valuably — what effect size the design could detect. It cannot show the flip did or did not create bookings. Any write-up must carry that on its face, and nothing from it may enter `wiki/experiments/` as a prior.

## The six stress tests

**1. Parallel trends across "a different kind of trip".** The analyst's own words are close to a refutation of the *level* DiD. Near-term 2026 departures booked in August are peak-season, high-volume, short-lead; 2027 departures booked in August are a thin, flat, long-lead series. A common multiplicative shock (weather, macro, competitor pricing, a pay week) then produces very different absolute movements, and the DiD reads the difference as effect. Recommendations, in order of strength:

- **Do not run this in levels.** Use a log or Poisson/log-link DiD so the assumption becomes *common proportional* trends, which is the assumption the business story actually implies. Say on the page which scale you are claiming — log-DiD and level-DiD are different estimands and one can be flat while the other trends.
- **One pre-period month (July 2026) is the design's worst weakness and the most fixable one.** An event study with "leads" needs many pre-periods. Ask for 18–24 months of booking-date series, and check ratio stability across all of it, not just the month before.
- **Replace the lumped "2027+" group with finer departure-month cohorts and let a synthetic control weight them** (booking-week × departure-month panel, donor pool = departure months outside 2026, pre-fit quality reported). A weighted donor set can match the treated cohorts' seasonal shape; a 1:1 comparison to "everything from 2027 onwards" cannot.
- **Better still, a control that is not a different kind of trip at all:** `avios_balance` is pre-treatment and gates whether the flip could bite. Members with near-zero balances cannot respond to a better conversion rate, so they are an untreated group *inside* the same trips and the same seasonality. A triple difference (departure-year group × period × can-respond) is the strongest design available here. It needs `avios_balance` to be genuinely observed — currently marked `observed: true` as an *assumption*, `confirmed_by: null`. That is worth one question to the analyst.

**2. Is the boundary sharp, and would RD beat DiD?** The rule is sharp; the *threshold* is arbitrary in exactly the way RD wants — a 30 Dec 2026 and a 3 Jan 2027 departure are nearly the same trip. So on comparability, RD in departure date around 31 Dec 2026 dominates the whole-group DiD. Two problems, one fatal on its own:

- The outcome is a **count of bookings by departure date**, so the density of the running variable *is* the outcome. You cannot use density continuity as the falsification test and the estimate at the same time, and manipulation (members shifting departure dates) is indistinguishable from effect. ### Cell 5 — the generator, one line per edge

18-month pre-period, daily panel at booking-date × departure-year-group. The two groups are given **different levels, seasonal amplitudes and trends** on purpose — that is your "different kind of trip", and a generator without it would prove the estimator works in a world we know we're not in.

```python
START, END = pd.Timestamp("2025-02-01"), pd.Timestamp("2026-09-30")
FLIP_START, FLIP_END = pd.Timestamp("2026-08-01"), pd.Timestamp("2026-08-14")
dates = pd.date_range(START, END, freq="D")

BREAK_PARALLEL_TRENDS = False   # flip to True to check the diagnostics actually catch it

def simulate(true_lift=TRUE_LIFT, break_pt=BREAK_PARALLEL_TRENDS, rng=rng):
    rows = []
    doy = dates.dayofyear.values
    t = (dates - START).days.values / 365.0
    shared_season = 0.22 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * (doy - 20) / 365.0)   # unobserved demand
    shock = rng.normal(0, 0.05, len(dates))

    for group, is_2026 in [("depart_2026", 1), ("depart_2027plus", 0)]:
        lead_days = 150 if is_2026 else 480
        base  = np.log(1800) if is_2026 else np.log(260)
        amp   = 1.0 if is_2026 else 0.55
        trend = 0.06 if is_2026 else 0.02
        if break_pt:
            trend += 0.25 * is_2026
        treated = ((dates >= FLIP_START) & (dates <= FLIP_END)).astype(int) * is_2026
        log_mu = base + amp*shared_season + trend*t + shock + np.log1p(treated*true_lift)
        bookings = rng.poisson(np.exp(log_mu))

        base_share = 0.30 if is_2026 else 0.26
        share = np.clip(base_share + treated * TRUE_SUBSTITUTION, 0, 1)
        redeeming = rng.binomial(bookings, share)

        rows.append(pd.DataFrame({
            "booking_date": dates, "departure_group": group, "treated_group": is_2026,
            "in_window": ((dates >= FLIP_START) & (dates <= FLIP_END)).astype(int),
            "treated": treated, "booking_departure_lead_time": lead_days,
            "member_booking_volume": bookings, "avios_redeeming_bookings": redeeming}))
    df = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
    df["non_redeeming_bookings"] = df.member_booking_volume - df.avios_redeeming_bookings
    return df

df = simulate()
print(df.groupby("departure_group").member_booking_volume.agg(["count","mean","std"]))
```

### Cell 11 — the substitution check

```python
def did_on(col, d=df):
    dd = d.copy(); dd["date_f"] = dd.booking_date.dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    mm = smf.glm(f"{col} ~ treated + C(departure_group) + C(date_f)",
                 data=dd, family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit(cov_type="HC1")
    return np.expm1(mm.params["treated"]), mm.pvalues["treated"]

for col in ["member_booking_volume", "avios_redeeming_bookings", "non_redeeming_bookings"]:
    e, pp = did_on(col); print(f"  {col:28s} {e:+7.2%}  (p={pp:.4f})")
print("\nTotal is the finding; the split is the diagnosis. Redeeming up with total flat")
print("= substitution. Both up together = genuine incremental volume.")
```
